title: Life Processes – II: Control and Coordination
summary: The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, sense organs and nerves) and the endocrine system (glands that pour chemical messengers called hormones directly into the blood) work together as a team to control and coordinate all our activities — physical actions, thinking and emotions. Eating, for example, involves seeing food, moving hands to the mouth, feeling full, and secreting digestive juices at the right time. A stimulus is any change that starts a response — touch, pressure, sound, light, heat, cold, chemicals.

The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Its dendrites (branched projections) receive impulses; the cell body has a nucleus and cytoplasm; the long axon (nerve fibre), covered by a fatty sheath with gaps called nodes of Ranvier, carries the impulse away and ends in bulbs that store chemicals called neurotransmitters. The junction between two neurons is a synapse, with a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft. When an impulse reaches the end of an axon, the neurotransmitter is released, crosses the cleft and starts an impulse in the next neuron, and finally in a muscle or gland. Types: sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (sense organs) to the brain or spinal cord; motor neurons carry them from the brain or spinal cord to effectors (muscles or glands); association (connecting) neurons in the brain and spinal cord link the two.

A nerve is a bundle of axons in a sheath, like an electric cable with insulated wires. Sensory nerves bring impulses to the brain or spinal cord (optic nerve); motor nerves carry them to muscles or glands; mixed nerves contain both (spinal nerves). There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves (from the brain) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (from the spinal cord).

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The brain lies in the bony cranium and is covered by three meninges — the tough outer dura mater, the delicate web-like arachnoid and the inner, blood-rich pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid between them cushions the brain against shocks. Meningitis is a contagious inflammation of the meninges caused by microbes (high fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light).

The cerebrum, the largest part, has two hemispheres with a folded grey cortex (cell bodies) over inner white matter (axons); it is the seat of intelligence, thinking, memory, reasoning, consciousness and will, and controls voluntary actions. The cerebellum, below the cerebrum, maintains balance and coordinates muscular movements (a drunk person walks clumsily because alcohol affects it). The medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain (part of the hind-brain), continues as the spinal cord and controls involuntary actions — heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis; injury to it can be fatal. The hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger and the pituitary.

The spinal cord runs from the medulla down the neural canal of the backbone, covered by the same three meninges. Its grey matter (cell bodies) is inside and white matter (axons) outside — the reverse of the brain — with a central canal of cerebrospinal fluid. Functions: (1) it controls reflex actions below the neck; (2) it carries sensory impulses from the skin and muscles to the brain; (3) it carries motor impulses from the brain to the muscles of the trunk and limbs.

A reflex action is a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without the involvement of the brain — withdrawing the hand from a hot object or a needle, closing the eyes in a dust storm, tears washing out dust, shivering in cold, sweating in heat. Natural (inborn) reflexes need no learning — breathing, swallowing, coughing, blinking. Conditioned (acquired) reflexes are learnt from experience, e.g. the mouth watering at the smell of favourite food; they fade unless reinforced. The path of a reflex is the reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (association neuron) → motor neuron → effector (muscle or gland) → response.

The peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects the CNS with the rest of the body. Its somatic part (cranial and spinal nerves) controls voluntary actions of skeletal muscles. Its autonomic part, chains of nerves and ganglia beside the backbone, controls involuntary actions of internal organs: the sympathetic system prepares the body for stress ('fight or flight' with adrenaline) — faster heartbeat, dilated pupils, sugar released from the liver; the parasympathetic system restores normal conditions — saliva and tears, digestion. The two are complementary.

A hormone is a chemical secreted by an endocrine gland and carried by the blood to a target organ elsewhere, where it causes a specific effect; too much or too little causes disease. Pituitary (at the base of the brain): growth hormone — too little causes dwarfism, too much gigantism; gonad-stimulating hormones make the ovaries produce oestrogen and progesterone and the testes produce testosterone at puberty, bringing secondary sexual characters; hyperactivity causes Cushing's disease. Thyroid (in the neck): its hormone (thyroxine) controls the rate of metabolism, growth and development — overactivity is hyperthyroidism, underactivity hypothyroidism; cretinism is severely stunted physical and mental growth from thyroid deficiency; simple goitre (swelling of the neck) is caused by lack of iodine, prevented by iodised salt. Pancreas: insulin and glucagon control blood glucose; too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus. Adrenal glands secrete adrenaline in emergencies; ovaries and testes secrete sex hormones.

objective: Read the passage and answer: 'The nervous system and the endocrine system work together as a team to control and coordinate all our activities. Sometimes we may not even be aware of their role in our health and well-being, and in our response to an urgent or dangerous situation.' (a) Name the two systems that control and coordinate all our body activities. (b) Which of these is usually executed in response to a dangerous situation? (A) Feeling of hunger (B) Role of digestive juices (C) Picking up food with the fingers (D) Immediate removal of the hand from a hot object
(a) The nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system. (b) (D) Immediate removal of the hand from a hot object (a reflex action).

Read the passage and answer: 'The brain is well protected within the bony cranium. It is further protected by three meninges — dura mater (outermost, tough), arachnoid (delicate middle layer) and pia mater (innermost, highly vascular).' (1) Name the innermost meninx. (2) What is the function of the fluid present between the meninges?
(1) Pia mater. (2) Cerebrospinal fluid acts as a cushion that protects the brain from shocks (and helps exchange of materials).
Fill in the blanks: The central nervous system consists of the ________ and the ________.
Match: (1) Cerebellum (2) Medulla oblongata — (a) intelligence and memory (b) balance and coordination of muscles (c) heartbeat and breathing (d) reflexes below the neck
Write True (T) or False (F): (1) Reflex actions are controlled by the cerebrum. (2) Hormones are carried to their target organs by the blood.
(1) False — they are controlled by the spinal cord. (2) True

case.passage: When your hand accidentally touches a hot pan, you pull it away at once, even before you feel pain. Such quick, automatic responses are called reflex actions. The receptor in the skin sends an impulse along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord, where an association neuron passes it to a motor neuron, which makes the muscles of the arm contract. Messages from one neuron to the next cross a small gap called a synapse with the help of chemicals.

vsa: Define nerves. Differentiate between sensory nerves and motor nerves with examples.

A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres (axons) enclosed in a sheath, which carries impulses. Sensory nerves carry impulses from sense organs to the brain or spinal cord (e.g. the optic nerve); motor nerves carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to muscles or glands (e.g. nerves to the eye muscles).
What is a reflex action? Give two examples.

A reflex action is a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without the involvement of the brain. Examples: withdrawing the hand from a hot object; blinking or tears flowing when dust enters the eye.
Differentiate between the cerebrum and the cerebellum.

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, with two hemispheres; it controls thinking, memory, intelligence and voluntary actions. The cerebellum is smaller, below the cerebrum; it maintains balance and coordinates muscular movements.
What is a hormone? Name the hormone whose shortage causes diabetes.
A hormone is a chemical secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which carries it to a target organ elsewhere to produce a specific effect. Insulin (from the pancreas).
Name the two parts of the autonomic nervous system and give one function of each.
Sympathetic — prepares the body for emergencies (faster heartbeat, dilated pupils). Parasympathetic — restores normal conditions (slows the heartbeat, promotes saliva and digestion).
Why does injury to the medulla oblongata often result in death?
The medulla controls vital involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing; if it is injured these may stop.
sa: Name the three types of neurons and write their functions.

(1) Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (sense organs) to the brain or spinal cord. (2) Motor neurons carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to effectors (muscles or glands). (3) Association (connecting) neurons, in the brain and spinal cord, connect sensory and motor neurons.
Write three functions of the spinal cord.

(1) It controls reflex actions of the body below the neck. (2) It conducts sensory impulses from the skin and muscles to the brain. (3) It conducts motor impulses from the brain to the muscles of the trunk and limbs.
Draw the generalised structure of a neuron and label dendrites, cell body, axon and nucleus.

Diagram: a cell body (cyton) containing a nucleus, with short branched dendrites on one side; from the other side a long axon covered by a sheath with nodes of Ranvier, ending in branched axon terminals (bulbs). Labels: dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon.

or: (a) Name the hormone released by the thyroid gland and its function. (b) Define hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism.

(a) Thyroxine; it controls the rate of metabolism and is needed for growth and development. (b) Hyperthyroidism: the thyroid is overactive and makes more hormone than needed. Hypothyroidism: the thyroid is underactive and makes less hormone than needed (in children it can cause cretinism).

sa: Draw a diagram of a synapse and label the synaptic vesicle, synaptic cleft, synaptic bulb and mitochondrion.

Diagram: the swollen end (synaptic bulb) of one neuron's axon lies close to the dendrite of the next neuron, separated by a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft. Inside the bulb are small round synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter and a few mitochondria. When an impulse arrives the vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, which starts an impulse in the next neuron.

Draw an outline of the human body and show the position of the glands that secrete (i) testosterone (ii) insulin (iii) the hormone whose malfunction causes severely stunted physical and mental growth (iv) the hormone whose malfunction causes dwarfism.
(i) Testes — in the scrotum below the abdomen. (ii) Pancreas — in the abdomen below the stomach. (iii) Thyroid — in the neck (cretinism). (iv) Pituitary — at the base of the brain (growth hormone).
la: Define spinal reflex. Draw a labelled diagram of it.

A spinal reflex is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus that is controlled by the spinal cord without involving the brain, e.g. withdrawing the hand from a hot object. Diagram (reflex arc): a receptor in the skin of the hand → sensory neuron entering the spinal cord through the dorsal root → association (relay) neuron in the grey matter → motor neuron leaving through the ventral root → effector muscle in the arm, which contracts and pulls the hand away. The spinal cord section shows inner grey matter and outer white matter.
Draw a neat diagram of a nerve cell (neuron) and label the nucleus, axon, dendrites and node of Ranvier. Give a brief description of the nerve cell.

Diagram: cell body with nucleus, short branched dendrites, a long axon with a fatty sheath interrupted at nodes of Ranvier, ending in terminal branches. Description: the neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Dendrites receive impulses and pass them to the cell body; the axon carries the impulse away; at its end, neurotransmitters released at a synapse pass the impulse to the next neuron or to a muscle or gland. The sheath insulates the axon, and the nodes of Ranvier help in fast transmission.

Draw a sectional view of the human brain and label the part (i) whose infection causes meningitis (ii) which controls the beating of the heart (iii) which coordinates muscular movements (iv) which helps us memorise facts.

(i) Meninges — the three membranes (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater) covering the brain. (ii) Medulla oblongata — at the base of the brain, continuing into the spinal cord. (iii) Cerebellum — below the back of the cerebrum. (iv) Cerebrum — the large upper part with two folded hemispheres.
With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the internal structure of the spinal cord. State its functions.

In cross-section the spinal cord has an inner butterfly-shaped grey matter (cell bodies of neurons) surrounded by outer white matter (nerve fibres running to and from the brain), with a central canal filled with cerebrospinal fluid; it is covered by the dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater and lies in the neural canal of the backbone. Spinal nerves leave it through dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots. Functions: controls reflexes below the neck; carries sensory impulses to the brain; carries motor impulses from the brain to the trunk and limbs.
